name: Specific heat capacity
subject: Physics
aim: Find the specific heat capacity of a solid block by measuring the energy needed to raise its temperature.
outcome: c from the gradient of a temperature-against-energy graph, using E = mcΔθ.
safety: Heater and block stay hot after switch-off. Do not touch. Mop spills at once — mains electricity near water.
equipment_1: Metal block with two holes (aluminium or copper)
equipment_9: Small amount of water for the thermometer hole
step_1: Measure and record the mass of the block in kg.
step_2: Wrap the block in insulation and stand it on a heatproof mat.
step_3: Put the heater in the large hole and the thermometer in the small one, with a drop of water to improve contact.
step_4: Record the starting temperature.
step_5: Switch on and start timing. Record temperature and energy every minute for 10 minutes.
step_6: Switch off, but keep recording for two more minutes — the temperature keeps rising.
step_7: Plot temperature against energy supplied.
maths_link: Rearranging E = mcΔθ; gradient of a straight line; units.
notes: Thermal energy escaping is the main systematic error — always mention insulation in the evaluation.

name: Thermal insulation
subject: Physics
aim: Investigate how the thickness or type of material affects the rate at which water cools.
outcome: A cooling curve per material; the best insulator gives the smallest temperature drop.
safety: Hot water — use water no hotter than 80 C with under-14s. Carry the beaker with two hands.
equipment_5: Insulating materials (bubble wrap, felt, newspaper, foam)
step_1: Wrap the beaker in one layer of the material and fix it with an elastic band.
step_2: Measure out the same volume of hot water each time.
step_3: Put the lid and thermometer in place and start the stopwatch.
step_4: Record the temperature every minute for 10 minutes.
step_5: Repeat with a second layer, then a third — or with a different material.
step_6: Plot all cooling curves on the same axes.
step_7: Compare the temperature drop over the full 10 minutes.
maths_link: Rate of change; reading a curve; fair-test control variables.
notes: The one required practical that runs in a normal room. Same volume, same starting temperature, same lid every time.

name: Resistance of a wire
subject: Physics
aim: Investigate how the resistance of a wire depends on its length.
outcome: Resistance is directly proportional to length — a straight line through the origin.
safety: The wire gets hot. Keep the current low and disconnect between readings. Do not touch the wire while the circuit is on.
equipment_1: Nichrome wire (about 1 m, taped to a metre rule)
equipment_6: Low-voltage power supply or battery pack
step_1: Tape the wire alongside the metre rule.
step_2: Build a series circuit: supply, switch, ammeter, wire. Put the voltmeter across the wire.
step_3: Clip the crocodile clips 100 mm apart.
step_4: Close the switch, read current and potential difference, then open it again.
step_5: Repeat for 200, 300 ... up to 1000 mm.
step_6: Work out R = V/I for each length.
step_7: Plot resistance against length and draw a line of best fit.
maths_link: R = V/I; direct proportion; line of best fit through the origin.
notes: Why current is kept low: a hot wire has a higher resistance, which bends the graph.

name: I–V characteristics
subject: Physics
aim: Find the current–potential difference graphs for a resistor, a filament lamp and a diode.
outcome: Straight line for the resistor, S-curve for the lamp, one-way step for the diode.
safety: Do not exceed the component ratings. The lamp gets hot.
step_1: Build a series circuit with the component, ammeter, variable resistor and supply.
step_2: Connect the voltmeter across the component only.
step_3: Set the variable resistor to its highest value and close the switch.
step_4: Record current and potential difference, then adjust and repeat for about eight settings.
step_5: Reverse the supply connections and repeat for negative values.
step_6: Swap in the next component and repeat.
step_7: Plot I against V for all three on separate axes.
maths_link: Gradient and its reciprocal; interpreting non-linear graphs.
notes: The diode always needs a protective resistor in series or it burns out.

name: Density
subject: Physics
aim: Measure the density of regular solids, irregular solids and liquids.
outcome: ρ = m/V for each sample; the displacement method for anything awkwardly shaped.
safety: Water and balances — wipe up spills. Take care with the eureka can spout.
step_1: Measure the mass of the object.
step_2: For a regular solid, measure its dimensions and calculate the volume.
step_3: For an irregular solid, fill the eureka can to the spout and let it settle.
step_4: Lower the object in gently and collect the displaced water in a measuring cylinder.
step_5: Read the volume at the bottom of the meniscus, at eye level.
step_6: For a liquid, find the mass of an empty cylinder, add the liquid, and find the mass again.
step_7: Calculate ρ = m/V and compare with published values.
maths_link: Rearranging formulas; unit conversion between g/cm3 and kg/m3.
notes: Runs perfectly well on a library table. The scales (I030) and ruler are already on the items list.

name: Force and extension (Hooke’s law)
subject: Physics
aim: Investigate how the extension of a spring depends on the force applied.
outcome: A straight line up to the limit of proportionality; spring constant from the gradient.
safety: Wear eye protection. Put a mat or tray under the masses, and never stand with feet under the hanger.
step_1: Clamp the stand to the bench and hang the spring from it.
step_2: Record the unloaded length of the spring against the ruler.
step_3: Add a 100 g mass and record the new length once it stops moving.
step_4: Repeat, adding masses one at a time, up to about eight.
step_5: Extension = loaded length minus original length.
step_6: Force = mass in kg x 9.8.
step_7: Plot force against extension and find the gradient — that is the spring constant.
step_8: Note where the line stops being straight: the limit of proportionality.
maths_link: F = ke; gradient; identifying where a linear model breaks down.
notes: A brilliant demonstration of "the maths only works in a range".

name: Force and acceleration
subject: Physics
aim: Investigate how acceleration depends on force and on mass.
outcome: a is proportional to F for a fixed mass, and inversely proportional to m for a fixed force.
safety: Catch the falling masses — do not let them land on feet. Clamp the pulley firmly.
equipment_6: Light gates and datalogger (or ticker tape and timer)
step_1: Set up the runway with the pulley at one end and the landing box beneath it.
step_2: Tilt the runway slightly to compensate for friction until the trolley moves at a steady speed when nudged.
step_3: Attach the string from the trolley over the pulley to the hanger.
step_4: Keep the total mass constant: move masses from the trolley to the hanger, not on to it.
step_5: Release the trolley and record the acceleration from the light gates.
step_6: Repeat for a range of accelerating forces.
step_7: Then keep the force constant and add mass to the trolley instead.
step_8: Plot a against F, and a against 1/m.
maths_link: Direct and inverse proportion; F = ma.
notes: The mass is moved, not added, so total mass stays constant. Examiners ask this constantly.

name: Waves
subject: Physics
aim: Measure the frequency, wavelength and speed of waves in a ripple tank and on a string.
outcome: v = f λ verified in two different media.
safety: Water and mains electricity — use a low-voltage supply. Warn anyone photosensitive before using a strobe.
equipment_4: White card or paper for the screen
step_1: Set the ripple tank level and add water to a shallow, even depth.
step_2: Switch on the dipper and the lamp; project the pattern on to the card below.
step_3: Freeze the pattern with the strobe or a slow-motion video.
step_4: Measure the length of ten wavelengths and divide by ten.
step_5: Read the frequency from the signal generator.
step_6: Calculate v = f λ.
step_7: For the string, hang masses over a pulley to tension it and find the frequency that gives a clear standing wave.
step_8: Wavelength is twice the distance between adjacent nodes. Calculate v again.
maths_link: v = f λ; measuring ten and dividing to reduce error.
notes: Filming on a phone at 240 fps replaces the strobe and is usually easier.

name: Light: reflection and refraction
subject: Physics
aim: Investigate reflection at a mirror and refraction through a glass block.
outcome: Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection; the ray bends towards the normal entering glass.
safety: The ray box lamp gets hot. Dim the room but keep walkways clear.
equipment_1: Ray box with a single slit
equipment_8: Power supply for the ray box
step_1: Put the paper down and draw round the block or mirror.
step_2: Draw the normal at 90 degrees to the surface where the ray will enter.
step_3: Shine a single ray at the surface at about 30 degrees to the normal.
step_4: Mark the incoming ray with two crosses and the outgoing ray with two more.
step_5: Remove the block and join the crosses to reconstruct the ray path.
step_6: Measure the angles of incidence, reflection and refraction from the normal.
step_7: Repeat for 20, 30, 40, 50 and 60 degrees.
step_8: Tabulate and look for the pattern.
maths_link: Angle measurement; the normal as a reference line; ratios.
notes: Needs only a ray box on top of what is already on the items list. A protractor (I006) is essential.

name: Infrared radiation
subject: Physics
aim: Investigate how the surface of an object affects the infrared radiation it emits or absorbs.
outcome: Matt black emits and absorbs most; shiny silver least.
safety: Boiling water inside the cube. Fill it carefully and do not move it once filled.
equipment_3: Infrared detector or thermopile (or an infrared thermometer)
step_1: Stand the Leslie cube on a heatproof mat and fill it with hot water.
step_2: Let it stand for two minutes so every face reaches the same temperature.
step_3: Set the detector a fixed distance from one face — 10 cm works well.
step_4: Record the reading for the matt black face.
step_5: Move the cube, not the detector, and repeat for the shiny black, matt white and shiny silver faces.
step_6: Keep the distance identical every time.
step_7: Repeat the whole set twice more and take a mean.
maths_link: Means; controlling distance as a variable.
notes: An infrared thermometer from a hardware shop is a cheap substitute for a thermopile.

name: Making a soluble salt
subject: Chemistry
aim: Prepare a pure, dry sample of a soluble salt from an insoluble oxide or carbonate and an acid.
outcome: Blue copper sulfate crystals, filtered and left to crystallise.
safety: Dilute sulfuric acid is an irritant — goggles throughout. Hot evaporating basins and Bunsen flames.
equipment_4: Bunsen burner, tripod, gauze, heatproof mat
step_1: Put 25 cm3 of dilute sulfuric acid in a beaker and warm it gently. Do not boil.
step_2: Turn off the Bunsen and add copper oxide a spatula at a time, stirring.
step_3: Keep adding until no more dissolves and some solid stays at the bottom — the acid is now used up.
step_4: Filter the mixture to remove the excess copper oxide.
step_5: Pour the blue filtrate into an evaporating basin.
step_6: Heat gently to concentrate it, stopping when crystals start to form at the edge.
step_7: Leave to crystallise slowly, then pat the crystals dry between filter papers.
maths_link: Excess reagent; percentage yield.
notes: Slow crystallisation gives bigger, better crystals. Heating to dryness ruins them.

name: Titration
subject: Chemistry
aim: Find the volume of acid needed to neutralise a known volume of alkali.
outcome: Concordant titres within 0.10 cm3, and a concentration calculated from them.
safety: Goggles throughout. Fill the burette below eye level using a funnel. Report all spills.
step_1: Rinse the burette with the acid and the pipette with the alkali.
step_2: Pipette 25.0 cm3 of alkali into the conical flask and add three drops of indicator.
step_3: Fill the burette, remove the funnel, and record the initial reading to 0.05 cm3.
step_4: Stand the flask on the white tile and run acid in, swirling continuously.
step_5: Do a rough titration first to find the approximate endpoint.
step_6: Repeat, adding dropwise near the endpoint, until one drop turns the solution colourless.
step_7: Record the final reading and repeat until two titres agree within 0.10 cm3.
step_8: Mean the concordant titres only, then use n = cV.
maths_link: Moles, concentration and volume; means excluding outliers; decimal places.
notes: The single most transferable maths practical in chemistry — good for a Higher-tier student who needs moles practice.

name: Electrolysis
subject: Chemistry
aim: Investigate what is produced at each electrode when aqueous solutions are electrolysed.
outcome: Metal or hydrogen at the cathode, halogen or oxygen at the anode, predicted from the reactivity series.
safety: Chlorine gas — use a fume cupboard or a very small volume in a well-ventilated room. Goggles throughout.
step_1: Half-fill the cell with copper sulfate solution.
step_2: Clamp the two graphite electrodes so they do not touch.
step_3: Connect to the d.c. supply at about 4 V and switch on.
step_4: Watch both electrodes: note any coating, bubbling or colour change.
step_5: Test any gas — a glowing splint relights in oxygen; damp litmus is bleached by chlorine.
step_6: Switch off, rinse everything and repeat with sodium chloride solution.
step_7: Write half equations for each electrode.
maths_link: Half equations; balancing charge.
notes: Must be d.c. Alternating current gives nothing useful and confuses the write-up.

name: Temperature changes
subject: Chemistry
aim: Investigate the temperature change when acid reacts with alkali in different proportions.
outcome: A peak temperature at the neutralisation point.
safety: Dilute acid and alkali — goggles and no skin contact. Use low concentrations with younger students.
equipment_2: Second cup or beaker for insulation
step_1: Stand the polystyrene cup inside the beaker for insulation.
step_2: Measure 30 cm3 of acid into the cup and record its starting temperature.
step_3: Add 5 cm3 of alkali, stir, and record the highest temperature reached.
step_4: Add another 5 cm3 and record the new highest temperature.
step_5: Continue in 5 cm3 steps up to 40 cm3 of alkali.
step_6: Plot temperature against volume of alkali added.
step_7: The peak of the graph is the neutralisation point.
maths_link: Reading a maximum from a graph; interpolation.
notes: Exothermic and endothermic made visible. Works on a library table with cheap kit.

name: Rates of reaction
subject: Chemistry
aim: Investigate how concentration affects the rate of a reaction, by two different methods.
outcome: Rate increases with concentration; a 1/time graph against concentration.
safety: Sulfur dioxide is produced in the thiosulfate method — ventilate the room and keep volumes small. Goggles throughout.
equipment_4: Paper with a black cross drawn on it
equipment_8: Gas syringe (for the marble chip method)
step_1: Draw a black cross on paper and stand the flask on it.
step_2: Measure 50 cm3 of thiosulfate into the flask.
step_3: Add 10 cm3 of acid and start the stopwatch at the moment of mixing.
step_4: Look down through the flask and stop the clock when the cross disappears.
step_5: Repeat with the thiosulfate diluted — 40 cm3 solution to 10 cm3 water, and so on.
step_6: Keep the total volume the same every time.
step_7: Plot 1/time against concentration.
maths_link: Rate as 1/time; proportionality; controlling total volume.
notes: Everyone judges "disappeared" slightly differently — same person watching every run.

name: Chromatography
subject: Chemistry
aim: Separate the dyes in inks and calculate Rf values.
outcome: A chromatogram with separated spots and an Rf value for each.
safety: Low hazard. If a solvent other than water is used, ventilate and keep away from flames.
equipment_9: Paper clip and rod to suspend the paper
step_1: Draw a pencil line 2 cm from the bottom of the paper. Pencil, never pen.
step_2: Spot each ink on the line, letting each spot dry before adding more.
step_3: Pour water into the beaker to a depth of about 1 cm.
step_4: Hang the paper so the bottom edge is in the water but the pencil line is above it.
step_5: Cover with the watch glass and leave undisturbed.
step_6: Remove the paper before the solvent front reaches the top, and mark the front immediately.
step_7: Measure the distance moved by each spot and by the solvent front.
step_8: Rf = distance moved by spot / distance moved by solvent front.
maths_link: Ratios; values always between 0 and 1.
notes: No lab needed. Rf is a good ratio exercise for a student who finds ratio abstract.

name: Identifying ions
subject: Chemistry
aim: Use flame tests and chemical tests to identify metal ions and non-metal ions.
outcome: A flame colour and a precipitate colour for each unknown.
safety: Bunsen flames and concentrated-ish solutions. Goggles, tied hair, no loose sleeves.
equipment_2: Nichrome wire loop or wooden splints
equipment_3: Dilute hydrochloric acid for cleaning the loop
equipment_9: Silver nitrate and dilute nitric acid
step_1: Clean the wire loop in acid and hold it in a blue flame until no colour shows.
step_2: Dip it in the sample and hold it at the edge of a blue flame.
step_3: Record the colour: lithium red, sodium yellow, potassium lilac, calcium orange-red, copper green.
step_4: For metal hydroxide tests, add sodium hydroxide solution dropwise to the sample in a test tube.
step_5: Record the precipitate colour, then add excess to see if it redissolves.
step_6: For carbonates, add acid and bubble the gas through limewater.
step_7: Match the results against a table of known ions.
maths_link: Systematic elimination; reading a results table.
notes: Flame tests are the memorable bit. The hydroxide precipitates carry more marks.

name: Analysis and purification of water
subject: Chemistry
aim: Analyse and purify water samples by testing pH, measuring dissolved solids, and distilling.
outcome: A pH, a mass of dissolved solids, and pure distilled water from a salty sample.
safety: Hot glassware and boiling water. Anti-bumping granules in the flask. Never seal the apparatus.
step_1: Test the pH of each sample with universal indicator or a probe.
step_2: Weigh a clean, dry evaporating basin.
step_3: Add a measured volume of sample and evaporate to dryness.
step_4: Reweigh to find the mass of dissolved solids.
step_5: Set up the distillation apparatus with the thermometer bulb level with the side arm.
step_6: Heat the salty sample and collect the distillate.
step_7: Test the distillate: it should be neutral and leave no solid on evaporation.
maths_link: Mass by difference; concentration in g per dm3.
notes: Ties neatly to a trip along the Wandle — pond, tap and bottled water side by side.

name: Microscopy
subject: Biology
aim: Use a light microscope to observe and draw plant or animal cells, and calculate magnification.
outcome: A labelled biological drawing with a magnification and a real size calculation.
safety: Coverslips and slides break and cut. Mounted needles are sharp. No cheek cells without a risk assessment.
equipment_10: Pencil and plain paper for the drawing
step_1: Peel a thin layer of onion epidermis with forceps.
step_2: Lay it flat on a slide and add one drop of iodine.
step_3: Lower the coverslip at an angle with a mounted needle to avoid air bubbles.
step_4: Start on the lowest objective lens and focus with the coarse focus.
step_5: Switch to a higher objective and use the fine focus only.
step_6: Draw what you see with clean, single pencil lines and no shading.
step_7: Magnification = eyepiece x objective.
step_8: Real size = image size / magnification. Watch the units.
maths_link: Standard form; unit conversion mm to μm; rearranging.
notes: A basic school microscope is around £60 and turns this into something you can run anywhere.

name: Microbiology
subject: Biology
aim: Investigate the effect of antiseptics or antibiotics on bacterial growth.
outcome: Clear zones of inhibition, measured and compared as areas.
safety: Strict aseptic technique. Incubate at 25 C maximum in a school, and never reopen a sealed plate.
equipment_2: Bacterial culture (E. coli or B. subtilis)
step_1: Sterilise the inoculating loop in a blue flame until red hot, then let it cool.
step_2: Spread the bacterial culture evenly across the agar surface.
step_3: Place the paper discs, each soaked in a different antiseptic, on the agar with sterile forceps.
step_4: Include a disc soaked in sterile water as the control.
step_5: Tape the lid on in two places — never seal it all the way round.
step_6: Incubate upside down at 25 C for 48 hours.
step_7: Measure the diameter of each clear zone and calculate its area with πr2.
maths_link: Area of a circle; comparing areas rather than diameters.
notes: Genuinely needs a school or college lab. Not one to run at a library.

name: Osmosis
subject: Biology
aim: Investigate the effect of sugar solution concentration on the mass of potato tissue.
outcome: A percentage change in mass graph crossing zero at the cell sap concentration.
safety: Cork borers and scalpels are sharp — cut on a board, away from the body. Adult supervision for under-14s.
equipment_3: Scalpel or knife and cutting board
step_1: Bore five cylinders from the same potato and trim them all to the same length.
step_2: Blot each one dry and record its starting mass.
step_3: Put one cylinder in each concentration and note the time.
step_4: Leave for at least 30 minutes — overnight is better.
step_5: Remove, blot dry the same way as before, and reweigh.
step_6: Percentage change = (change in mass / starting mass) x 100.
step_7: Plot percentage change against concentration and read off where the line crosses zero.
maths_link: Percentage change; reading an intercept; why percentages beat raw change.
notes: Blotting technique is the biggest source of error — same number of dabs every time.

name: Food tests
subject: Biology
aim: Use qualitative reagents to test for starch, sugars, proteins and lipids.
outcome: Four colour changes, each identifying one food group.
safety: Benedict’s needs a hot water bath, not a naked flame. Ethanol is highly flammable — no Bunsen anywhere near it. Check food allergies before handling any sample.
step_1: Grind the food with a little distilled water and filter it.
step_2: Starch: add a few drops of iodine. Orange to blue-black is positive.
step_3: Sugars: add Benedict’s and stand in the hot water bath for five minutes. Blue to brick red is positive.
step_4: Protein: add Biuret reagent. Blue to purple is positive.
step_5: Lipids: shake the sample with ethanol, then pour into water. A cloudy white emulsion is positive.
step_6: Record the starting and finishing colour for every test — not just the result.
maths_link: Qualitative versus quantitative data.
notes: Check allergies before this one, always. The lipid test uses ethanol, so it is lab-only.

name: Enzymes
subject: Biology
aim: Investigate the effect of pH on the rate at which amylase breaks down starch.
outcome: A rate-against-pH curve with an optimum.
safety: Iodine stains skin and clothes. Goggles. Buffer solutions are irritants.
equipment_3: Buffer solutions from pH 4 to pH 10
step_1: Put a drop of iodine in every well of the spotting tile.
step_2: Mix 2 cm3 starch, 2 cm3 amylase and 2 cm3 of one buffer in a test tube. Start the stopwatch.
step_3: Every 30 seconds, take a drop of the mixture and add it to the next iodine well.
step_4: Blue-black means starch is still present. Keep going until the drop stays orange.
step_5: Record the time taken for the starch to disappear.
step_6: Repeat for each pH.
step_7: Rate = 1000 / time. Plot rate against pH.
maths_link: Rate as a reciprocal of time; identifying an optimum from a curve.
notes: Keep the temperature constant with a water bath — otherwise two variables change at once.

name: Photosynthesis
subject: Biology
aim: Investigate the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis.
outcome: Rate against 1/d2, showing the inverse square relationship.
safety: Lamp and water together — keep the supply away from the beaker. The lamp gets hot.
equipment_6: Beaker of water as a heat shield
step_1: Cut a fresh piece of pondweed and put it in the boiling tube, cut end upwards.
step_2: Fill the tube with sodium hydrogencarbonate solution to supply carbon dioxide.
step_3: Place the beaker of water between the lamp and the tube to absorb heat.
step_4: Set the lamp 10 cm away and leave for five minutes to settle.
step_5: Count the bubbles released in one minute. Repeat three times and take a mean.
step_6: Move the lamp to 20, 30, 40 and 50 cm and repeat.
step_7: Plot rate against 1/d2 rather than against distance.
maths_link: Inverse square law; means; why 1/d2 straightens the graph.
notes: The heat shield is what stops temperature becoming a second variable.

name: Reaction time
subject: Biology
aim: Measure the effect of a factor on human reaction time.
outcome: A mean reaction time in seconds, before and after the factor changes.
safety: None beyond the obvious. Do not test caffeine on under-16s.
equipment_4: Conversion table or the formula t = √(2d/g)
equipment_8: Tablet or laptop with a reaction-time test
step_1: Sit with your forearm flat on the table and your hand over the edge, thumb and finger 1 cm apart.
step_2: Your partner holds the ruler with the zero mark level with your thumb.
step_3: They drop it without warning; you catch it as fast as you can.
step_4: Record the number the top of your thumb lands on.
step_5: Repeat ten times and discard the first two attempts as practice.
step_6: Convert distance to time using t = √(2d/g).
step_7: Change one factor — a distraction, background noise — and repeat.
maths_link: Means; converting a distance to a time; anomalies.
notes: Zero kit beyond a ruler. The best required practical for a first session with a nervous student.

name: Plant responses and germination
subject: Biology
aim: Investigate the effect of light or gravity on the growth of newly germinated seedlings.
outcome: Shoots bend towards light; roots grow downwards regardless of orientation.
safety: Wash hands after handling seeds and compost. Some seeds are treated — use untreated cress.
equipment_5: Cardboard box or foil to make a light source on one side only
equipment_10: Camera or phone for a time series
step_1: Line the petri dishes with damp cotton wool and scatter cress seeds evenly.
step_2: Leave them in the dark for two days to germinate.
step_3: Put one dish in all-round light, one in a box with a slit on one side, one in the dark.
step_4: Keep the cotton wool damp throughout.
step_5: Measure and photograph the seedlings every day for a week.
step_6: Record the height and the direction of bending.
step_7: Compare the three conditions.
maths_link: Measuring growth over time; angles of bending.
notes: Runs over a week, so it suits a holiday club better than a one-hour session.

name: Field investigations
subject: Biology
aim: Use sampling to estimate the population size of a species and study the effect of a factor on its distribution.
outcome: A population estimate for the whole area, and a transect showing how distribution changes.
safety: Outdoor risk assessment, high-vis, headcount at every stop. Wash hands afterwards. Never sample near the river edge.
step_1: Lay two tape measures at right angles to make a grid over the sample area.
step_2: Generate random coordinates and place the quadrat there — no choosing where to put it.
step_3: Count the number of the target species inside the quadrat.
step_4: Repeat for at least ten quadrats.
step_5: Mean per quadrat x (total area / quadrat area) = population estimate.
step_6: For the transect, lay one tape from shade into open ground and place quadrats at fixed intervals.
step_7: Plot abundance against distance along the transect.
maths_link: Means; scaling up a sample; area calculations; random sampling.
notes: Wandle Park or Colliers Wood Recreation Ground both work. Uses the trundle wheel (I023) and first aid kit (I022) already on the items list.

name: Decay
subject: Biology
aim: Investigate the effect of temperature on the rate of decay of fresh milk.
outcome: Time for the pink colour to disappear against temperature — faster when warmer, up to the point of denaturation.
safety: Lipase and sodium carbonate are irritants. Goggles. Do not drink anything. Dispose of milk properly.
equipment_5: Water baths at a range of temperatures
step_1: Put 5 cm3 of milk, 7 cm3 of sodium carbonate and five drops of phenolphthalein in a test tube. It turns pink.
step_2: Stand the tube in the first water bath and let it reach temperature.
step_3: Add 1 cm3 of lipase and start the stopwatch.
step_4: Stop the clock when the pink colour disappears — fatty acids have made it acidic.
step_5: Repeat at each temperature, keeping every volume the same.
step_6: Rate = 1000 / time. Plot rate against temperature.
maths_link: Rate as a reciprocal; optimum temperature.
notes: The pH change is the measurable thing here, not the smell.

name: Radius of the Earth from a tall building
subject: Maths
aim: Estimate the radius of the Earth by measuring how far away the horizon is from a high vantage point.
outcome: A value for R from R = d2 / 2h, usually within 20 per cent of 6371 km.
safety: A public viewing platform only — never a roof or a window ledge. Headcount before and after. Do not lean out.
equipment_1: A tall building with a public viewpoint and known height
equipment_2: Map or satellite view for measuring distance
step_1: Find a viewpoint of known height. Britannia Point in Colliers Wood is 59.5 m over 17 storeys.
step_2: From the top, identify the furthest landmark you can clearly see on the ground.
step_3: Measure the straight-line distance to it on a map.
step_4: That distance d, with the height h, gives R = d2 / 2h.
step_5: Convert everything to metres before substituting.
step_6: Compare with the accepted 6371 km and work out the percentage error.
step_7: Discuss why buildings and haze in London make the horizon hard to see, and what that does to d.
maths_link: Rearranging; standard form; percentage error; Pythagoras behind the formula.
notes: The example Halex asked for. In flat country you would use the sea horizon; in London you use the furthest identifiable landmark and accept a bigger error — which is itself the lesson.

name: Eratosthenes’ shadow
subject: Maths
aim: Estimate the circumference of the Earth from the length of a shadow at midday.
outcome: A circumference within about 10 per cent of 40 000 km.
safety: Sun safety — hats, shade, and never look at the sun. Chalk marks only on your own ground.
equipment_1: Metre stick or tall vertical pole
equipment_7: Clock set to local solar noon
equipment_8: Published shadow data from a second latitude
step_1: Stand the metre stick perfectly vertical on flat ground and check with the level.
step_2: About 15 minutes before local solar noon, mark the shadow tip every few minutes.
step_3: The shortest shadow is solar noon.
step_4: Measure the shortest shadow length and the stick height.
step_5: Angle = inverse tan (shadow / height). That is your angle from the sun.
step_6: Get the same angle for the same day from a place at a different latitude.
step_7: Difference in angles / 360 = distance between the places / circumference.
maths_link: Trigonometry; ratio and proportion; angles in parallel lines.
notes: Two schools in different cities measuring on the same day is the classic version. Published data works if you only have one site.

name: Height of a tree or tower by clinometer
subject: Maths
aim: Measure the height of something too tall to reach using an angle and a distance.
outcome: A height in metres, checked against a second measurement from a different distance.
safety: Watch for traffic and cyclists when pacing out distances. Stay off the road.
equipment_6: Metre stick for measuring eye height
equipment_7: Chalk or cones to mark positions
step_1: Stand where you can see the top of the tree clearly.
step_2: Measure your eye height from the ground.
step_3: Sight the top through the clinometer and read the angle of elevation.
step_4: Measure the horizontal distance from you to the base.
step_5: Height = distance x tan(angle) + eye height.
step_6: Move to a different distance and repeat.
step_7: If the two answers disagree, work out which measurement is most likely to blame.
maths_link: Tangent ratio; adding eye height; repeat measurement.
notes: Uses the clinometer (I027) and trundle wheel (I023) already owned. The best value-for-effort outdoor session there is.

name: Speed of light with a microwave and chocolate
subject: Physics
aim: Measure the speed of light using standing waves in a microwave oven.
outcome: A value near 3 x 10^8 m/s from c = 2 d f.
safety: Adult operates the microwave. Melted chocolate is hot. Remove the turntable first, and do not run the oven empty.
equipment_1: Microwave oven with the turntable removed
equipment_2: Large bar of chocolate or a plate of marshmallows
equipment_9: The frequency from the oven label, usually 2450 MHz
step_1: Take the turntable out so the food cannot rotate.
step_2: Lay the chocolate flat on the plate and put it in the oven.
step_3: Heat for 20 seconds — just long enough for the first melted patches to appear.
step_4: Measure the distance between the centres of two adjacent melted patches. That is half a wavelength.
step_5: Wavelength = 2 x that distance.
step_6: Read the frequency off the back of the oven, usually 2450 MHz.
step_7: c = f x wavelength. Compare with 3 x 10^8 m/s.
maths_link: Standard form; unit prefixes; v = f λ.
notes: The single best "the maths is real" demonstration for a reluctant student. Needs a microwave, so it suits a holiday event at the community centre.

name: Buffon’s needle
subject: Maths
aim: Estimate π by dropping matchsticks on to a set of parallel lines.
outcome: An estimate of π that improves visibly as the number of drops rises.
safety: None. Use matchsticks with the heads removed, or cocktail sticks with blunted ends.
equipment_1: Cocktail sticks or matchsticks, all the same length
equipment_10: Spreadsheet or the iPad for plotting
step_1: Rule parallel lines on the paper exactly one stick-length apart.
step_2: Drop the sticks on to the paper from a small height, one at a time or a handful at once.
step_3: Count the total dropped, N, and the number crossing a line, C.
step_4: π is approximately 2N / C.
step_5: Do 50 drops, then 100, then 500, pooling results across the group.
step_6: Plot the estimate against the number of drops.
step_7: Watch it converge — and note how slowly.
maths_link: Experimental probability; convergence; why large samples matter.
notes: Pool the whole group’s results to get to 1000 drops. The convergence graph is the real lesson.

name: Monte Carlo π with rice
subject: Maths
aim: Estimate π by scattering grains over a square with a quarter circle drawn in it.
outcome: π approximately 4 x (grains inside the arc / grains in total).
safety: Sweep up afterwards. Do not use rice with anyone who has a grain allergy — dried peas work too.
equipment_1: Square of card, at least 30 cm
step_1: Draw a square on the card and, from one corner, a quarter circle with radius equal to the side.
step_2: Stand the card in the tray.
step_3: Scatter rice evenly over the whole square from a height.
step_4: Count the grains inside the arc and the total on the card.
step_5: π is approximately 4 x inside / total.
step_6: Repeat with more grains and see the estimate settle.
step_7: Compare the accuracy with Buffon’s needle for the same effort.
maths_link: Area ratios; proportion; estimation.
notes: Uses the pair of compasses (I007) for the arc. Pairs well with PR-FN05 in the same session.

name: π from circles
subject: Maths
aim: Discover π as the gradient of circumference plotted against diameter.
outcome: A straight line through the origin with a gradient of about 3.14.
safety: None.
equipment_1: Ten round objects of different sizes
equipment_2: String or a flexible tape measure
step_1: Wrap the string once round each object and mark where it meets.
step_2: Straighten the string against the ruler to get the circumference.
step_3: Measure the diameter across the widest point.
step_4: Record both for all ten objects.
step_5: Plot circumference against diameter.
step_6: Draw the line of best fit through the origin.
step_7: Measure its gradient. That is π.
step_8: Divide C by d for each object as a check.
maths_link: Gradient; direct proportion; line of best fit; constants in maths.
notes: The moment a ten-year-old sees π appear from measuring jam jars is worth the whole session.

name: Monty Hall
subject: Maths
aim: Test whether switching doors really doubles your chance of winning.
outcome: Switching wins about two thirds of the time over 100+ trials.
safety: None.
equipment_2: A counter or sweet to hide
equipment_8: Tablet for a simulation to compare against
step_1: One person hides the counter under one of three cups while the other looks away.
step_2: The player picks a cup without lifting it.
step_3: The host lifts one of the other two cups, always revealing an empty one.
step_4: The player either sticks or switches. Record the choice and the result.
step_5: Do 50 trials always sticking, then 50 always switching.
step_6: Compare the two win rates.
step_7: Run a simulation for 10 000 trials and compare with your 100.
maths_link: Conditional probability; relative frequency; why intuition fails.
notes: The argument it starts is the point. Have the simulation ready for the student who refuses to believe the cups.

name: Perimeter of Wandle Park with a trundle wheel
subject: Maths
aim: Measure the perimeter of a real park and estimate its area.
outcome: A perimeter in metres and an area estimate, checked against a satellite measurement.
safety: Outdoor risk assessment, high-vis, headcount at every corner. Stay away from the river bank.
step_1: Print a satellite image of the park and mark the corners on it.
step_2: Walk the perimeter with the trundle wheel, recording each straight section separately.
step_3: Add the sections for the total perimeter.
step_4: Sketch the park as a set of rectangles and triangles on the map.
step_5: Measure the sides of each shape by pacing or by scaling off the map.
step_6: Calculate the area of each shape and add them.
step_7: Compare with the area given by an online map tool and discuss the difference.
maths_link: Perimeter; compound area; scale drawings; estimation.
notes: Uses the trundle wheel, tape measure, cones and first aid kit already on the items list.

name: Flow rate of the River Wandle
subject: Maths
aim: Estimate how much water passes a point on the Wandle every second.
outcome: A flow rate in cubic metres per second, from area x velocity.
safety: Never enter the water. Measure from a bridge or a fenced bank only. One adult per three students at the water’s edge. Wash hands afterwards.
equipment_1: Two oranges or tennis balls as floats
equipment_4: Metre stick for depth (used from a bridge)
step_1: Pick a straight stretch of the river with a bridge or a safe fenced bank.
step_2: Measure a 10 m length along the bank and mark both ends.
step_3: Drop a float in at the upstream mark and time it to the downstream mark.
step_4: Repeat five times and take a mean. Velocity = distance / mean time.
step_5: Measure the width, and the depth at three or four points across it.
step_6: Cross-sectional area = width x mean depth.
step_7: Flow rate = area x velocity, in cubic metres per second.
step_8: Compare with the Environment Agency figure for the Wandle.
maths_link: Means; compound measures; cross-sectional area; cubic metres per second.
notes: The Wandle runs straight past the Sainsbury’s footbridge — the landmark data already has it. Surface floats travel faster than the average, so the answer is always an overestimate. That is a discussion, not a flaw.

name: Spaghetti tower load test
subject: Maths
aim: Build the tallest tower that can carry a mass, then test it to destruction.
outcome: Height in cm and mass carried in g; a graph of the two across the group.
safety: Spaghetti snaps and flies. Eye protection during the load test. Sweep up — dry spaghetti on a floor is a slip hazard.
equipment_7: Small basket or cup to hold the masses
step_1: Give each team the same materials: 20 sticks, 20 marshmallows, one metre of tape.
step_2: Set a 20 minute build limit.
step_3: Measure each tower’s height.
step_4: Hang the basket from the top and add masses 50 g at a time.
step_5: Record the mass at which it fails.
step_6: Plot height against mass carried for every team.
step_7: Discuss why the tall thin ones fail first, and which shapes survived.
maths_link: Measurement; plotting two variables; triangles versus squares in structures.
notes: The best ice-breaker in the list. Triangles win, every time, and the students work out why themselves.

name: Terminal velocity of cupcake cases
subject: Physics
aim: Investigate how the mass of a falling object affects the speed at which it stops accelerating.
outcome: Time of fall against number of cases, showing terminal velocity rising with mass.
safety: Drop from a stepladder or a landing with a rail — never lean over a stairwell. One adult on the ladder.
equipment_4: Stepladder or a safe drop point of known height
equipment_6: Chalk to mark the drop line
step_1: Measure the drop height and mark the release point.
step_2: Drop one case and time its fall. Repeat five times and take a mean.
step_3: Nest two cases together and repeat.
step_4: Continue up to eight nested cases.
step_5: Terminal velocity = height / mean time.
step_6: Plot velocity against number of cases.
step_7: Film one drop in slow motion and find where the case stops speeding up.
maths_link: Means; speed = distance / time; proportionality.
notes: Cheap, safe, and shows air resistance beating gravity in real time.

name: Density tower
subject: Chemistry
aim: Layer liquids of different densities and test what floats in each.
outcome: A stable column of coloured layers, with objects suspended at different depths.
safety: Do not drink anything. Wipe up oil spills at once. Glass jar — use a plastic one with younger children.
equipment_1: Tall clear jar or measuring cylinder
equipment_7: Small objects (grape, bolt, cork, bead, ping-pong ball)
step_1: Weigh 50 ml of each liquid and calculate its density.
step_2: Predict the order of the layers from the densities alone.
step_3: Pour the densest liquid in first, then each next one gently down the side of the jar.
step_4: Let it settle between layers.
step_5: Drop the small objects in one at a time.
step_6: Record which layer each object comes to rest in.
step_7: Work out the density of each object from the layers it sits between.
maths_link: Density; ordering decimals; bounds and inequalities.
notes: The prediction step before pouring is what turns a party trick into a lesson.
